Facts checked in English: Statute of Anne, 8 Anne c. 19 (1710), at https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/anne_1710.asp (fourteen years, then the right returns to the author “if they are then living, for another term of fourteen years”; twenty-one years for books already printed); the Lords' vote to reverse the Chancery decree on February 22, 1774, at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donaldson_v_Becket. Camden's words in contenu_vulgarise (“the effects of the grossest tyranny and usurpation”) also match that page.

titre: Donaldson v. Becket, or the End of Perpetual Copyright
accroche: On February 22, 1774, the House of Lords denies London's booksellers an everlasting copyright: published books fall into the public domain.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1769, three judges to one side with London's booksellers: the poem *The Seasons*, by James Thomson, belongs to its publisher forever. Five years later, the House of Lords rules the opposite way. Between the two stand a 1710 statute that the booksellers refuse to read as it is written, and a Scottish bookseller who refuses to bow to it.

## A fourteen-year statute, a right meant to last forever

The Statute of Anne, an English law of 1710, protects a book for fourteen years, renewable once if the author is still alive. Books already published at that date receive twenty-one years. The booksellers, who hold most of the rights, want more. They argue that the statute created nothing: it merely added penalties to an older right, rooted in the common law, that never expires.

In 1769, in *Millar v. Taylor*, the Court of King's Bench sides with them by three votes to one; Justice Yates alone dissents. Thomas Becket relies on that precedent against Alexander Donaldson, a Scottish bookseller, over the same Thomson poem. The Court of Chancery grants the injunction on the strength of that precedent. Donaldson appeals to the Lords. About seven months earlier, the Court of Session of Scotland, in *Hinton v. Donaldson*, had held that Scots law recognized no common-law copyright.

## What the Lords decide, and what they are made to say

The appeal is argued in February 1774. Lord Apsley puts three questions to the judges, and Lord Camden adds two. Eleven of the twelve judges answer; Lord Mansfield abstains, having already judged *Millar*. Seven judges to four recognize the existence of a perpetual common-law right; historians still dispute the exact tally of the other answers.

The peers, however, do not follow the majority of their judges. On February 22, 1774, the House votes to reverse the Chancery decree. Five peers speak: Camden, Apsley, the Bishop of Carlisle and the Earl of Effingham argue for reversal, Lord Lyttleton against. Camden holds that the authorities the booksellers invoke, patents, privileges, Star Chamber decrees and Stationers' Company regulations, are “the effects of the grossest tyranny and usurpation.” The vote is taken by voice, without a division: no one will ever know who voted for what.

## A narrower reach than its legend

A voice vote yields no shared reasoning. Its certain effect is that published books fall under the terms of the English Statute of Anne and enter the public domain when those terms expire. Whether the Lords also denied any common-law right before publication remains debated by historians.

The booksellers do not give up. In the months that follow, they bring to Parliament a *Booksellers' Bill* that would give them back by statute what they have just lost before the Lords: the bill passes the House of Commons in 1774, then stalls before the Lords, who reject it. A year later, the Copyright Act of 1775 grants the English and Scottish universities, along with the colleges of Eton, Westminster and Winchester, a perpetual right to reprint, but only for books given or bequeathed to them. What the booksellers obtain neither from the judges nor from Parliament, these institutions obtain, within a far narrower frame.

repere.texte: The Statute of Anne (English law, 1710) protects a book for fourteen years, renewable once if the author is alive, and for twenty-one years for books already published. On February 22, 1774, the Lords vote to reverse the Chancery decree that had protected Becket against Donaldson with no limit of time.

carte.punch: In 1774, the Lords deny London's booksellers an everlasting copyright.
carte.idee: The booksellers argued that their right to a book came from the common law and never expired. On February 22, 1774, the House of Lords reverses the decision that had protected them: published books fall under the terms of the English statute of 1710 and then return to the public domain.

quiz.question: What is the certain effect of the Lords' vote of February 22, 1774?
choix: Booksellers keep forever the rights they bought from authors
Copyright in a published book now exists only in Scotland
Published books fall under the terms of the English Statute of Anne and then enter the public domain
Rights in published books pass to the kingdom's universities
quiz.explication: The Lords reverse the decree that protected Becket with no limit of time: published books follow the terms of the Statute of Anne and then enter the public domain. The booksellers do not keep an everlasting right; that is precisely what they lose. Scotland is involved only upstream, through the decision in Hinton v Donaldson. The universities obtain a perpetual right only in 1775, by statute, and only over works bequeathed to them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In 1769, in the case of Millar v. Taylor, what does the Court of King's Bench decide?
choix: By three votes to one, it recognizes a perpetual right for booksellers over Thomson's poem
Unanimously, it denies booksellers any perpetual right
It sends the case to the House of Lords without ruling
It holds that Scots law recognizes no common-law copyright
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Three judges to one, with Justice Yates alone dissenting, side with the booksellers: Thomson's poem would belong to them forever. That 1769 judgment then serves as the precedent in Becket v. Donaldson.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On February 22, 1774, how does the House of Lords vote to reverse the Chancery decree?
choix: By a roll-call vote, recording each peer's vote
By voice, without a division, so no one knows who voted for what
By the votes of the five peers who spoke alone
Unanimously among the peers present, with no declared opposition
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The vote is taken by voice and without a division, so the individual votes remain unknown; only five peers speak, with Lyttleton against, which does not describe the whole vote or its unanimity.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Copyright Act of 1775 grant the English and Scottish universities and the colleges of Eton, Westminster and Winchester?
choix: The same fourteen-year right as the Statute of Anne, but renewable indefinitely
A perpetual right over all books published in England, as the booksellers wanted
A perpetual right to reprint, but only for books given or bequeathed to them
A say over future copyright laws, in exchange for their support of the Lords
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1775 act gives them a perpetual right to reprint, but only for books given or bequeathed to them, a far narrower frame than the general right over all published books that the booksellers claimed in vain.
